cards.body: Scientists first decide what they want to discover. That question shapes the spacecraft, the instruments and the route.
cards.example: To study the Moon, a mission might ask: how hot and cold does the surface get?
cards.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
cards.title: Every mission starts with a question
cards.uncertainty: A mission can only answer the questions its instruments were designed for.

cards.body: Ideas grow from a rough concept to a reviewed design. JPL calls these steps Concept Maturity Levels (CML): Idea, Feasibility, Trade Studies and Point Design.
cards.example: You start with an objective, check if it is possible, compare options, then freeze a design.
cards.title: From idea to design review
cards.uncertainty: The four simplified stages stand in for a much longer real process with many reviews.

cards.body: A goal becomes measurable requirements: how much data, which instruments, how much power and fuel.
cards.example: Examining the Moon's temperature needs a thermal sensor and enough power to run it.
cards.title: Objectives become requirements
cards.uncertainty: Real requirements are far more detailed; this is a simplified version.

cards.body: Every instrument adds mass and uses power. Engineers balance what a mission can carry against what it can do.
cards.example: Adding a spectrometer means carrying more mass and drawing more electricity.
cards.title: Mass and power trade-offs
cards.uncertainty: The exact numbers depend on the spacecraft; the principle is what matters.

cards.body: Spare parts and backup systems help a spacecraft survive a failure, but they also add mass and complexity.
cards.example: The ISS keeps orbital replacement units that astronauts can swap in.
cards.title: Reliability and backups
cards.uncertainty: Backups add cost and mass; engineers must balance both sides.

cards.body: Spacecraft must survive both extreme cold and extreme heat. Insulation, heaters and radiators keep equipment in a safe range.
cards.example: A lander on Mars needs heaters and insulation for very cold nights.
cards.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
cards.title: Thermal protection
cards.uncertainty: Exact temperatures vary by orbit and season.

cards.body: The Martian atmosphere is mostly carbon dioxide and much thinner than Earth's, so it is very cold at the surface.
cards.example: Surface pressure on Mars is a tiny fraction of Earth's sea-level pressure.
cards.title: Mars has a thin atmosphere
cards.uncertainty: Values change with location and season on Mars.

cards.body: With no air to hold heat, the lunar surface gets very hot in sunlight and very cold in shadow.
cards.example: Apollo astronauts needed suits to cope with both extremes.
cards.title: The Moon has no atmosphere
cards.uncertainty: Small amounts of gas exist near the surface, but for practical purposes there is none.

cards.body: Earth's magnetic field deflects many charged particles from the Sun. The Moon and Mars have no strong global field.
cards.example: A magnetometer measures field strength in microtesla (uT).
cards.title: Magnetic fields protect planets
cards.uncertainty: Field strength varies from place to place around a planet.

cards.body: A spacecraft follows a curving path set by gravity and its speed. Engineers plan this path carefully before launch.
cards.example: Getting to Mars needs the right launch window and speed.
cards.title: Trajectories, not straight lines
cards.uncertainty: Real trajectories are computed with detailed gravity models; the map is simplified.

cards.body: To change course or slow down, a spacecraft burns propellant. Each change costs fuel, so fuel is planned like a budget.
cards.example: A course correction uses a small, planned burn of propellant.
cards.title: Changing speed costs propellant
cards.uncertainty: Real missions budget every burn carefully; the game abstracts this into fuel.

cards.body: Cameras capture images of surfaces, clouds and features. They are often the first instrument to reveal what a world looks like.
cards.example: Rovers photograph rocks and landscapes.
cards.title: Cameras
cards.uncertainty: Image quality depends on distance, light and the camera itself.

cards.body: Thermal sensors measure temperature by detecting heat (infrared light).
cards.example: They can show how hot a surface gets in sunlight.
cards.title: Thermal sensors
cards.uncertainty: Readings mix surface and near-surface air temperatures.

cards.body: A spectrometer splits light into colours to find out what a material or atmosphere is made of.
cards.example: Spectrometers identified water ice on other worlds.
cards.title: Spectrometers
cards.uncertainty: Results need careful calibration to interpret correctly.

cards.body: A magnetometer measures magnetic field strength, revealing whether a world is protected from charged particles.
cards.example: Measured in microtesla (uT).
cards.title: Magnetometers
cards.uncertainty: The spacecraft's own electronics can interfere, so calibration matters.

cards.body: Large dish antennas on Earth send commands to a spacecraft and receive its data. NASA's Deep Space Network uses stations around the world.
cards.example: A station can listen to a spacecraft even when it is very far away.
cards.title: Ground stations
cards.uncertainty: Coverage depends on which stations can see the spacecraft at that moment.

cards.body: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, but distances in space are huge, so there is always a delay.
cards.example: A signal to Mars can take several minutes to arrive.
cards.title: Signal delay
cards.uncertainty: Delay grows with distance; the exact time changes as planets move.

cards.body: Telemetry is the stream of measurements a spacecraft sends about its own health: temperature, power, battery and more.
cards.example: Engineers watch telemetry to spot a problem early.
cards.title: Telemetry
cards.uncertainty: Telemetry can only report what sensors measure, so some faults stay hidden.

cards.body: Before launch, engineers run checklists to confirm every system is ready. A green checklist means fewer surprises.
cards.example: Fuel, power and life support are checked together.
cards.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
cards.title: Readiness before launch
cards.uncertainty: Real checklists are far longer; the game shows the idea, not the paperwork.

cards.body: When the signal delay is long or the link is lost, a spacecraft must make some decisions on its own.
cards.example: A spacecraft can point its antenna or safe itself without waiting for Earth.
cards.title: Operating on its own
cards.uncertainty: Autonomy is limited on purpose so engineers stay in control of important decisions.

cards.body: Radiation, extreme temperatures and tiny high-speed dust grains (micrometeoroids) can all damage a spacecraft.
cards.example: Whipple shielding breaks up tiny grains before they reach the hull.
cards.title: Space is a hazardous place
cards.uncertainty: Risk can be reduced but never removed completely.

cards.body: A measurement is just a number. Scientists compare many measurements and models before drawing a conclusion.
cards.example: One temperature reading does not describe a whole planet.
cards.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
cards.title: Data is not knowledge
cards.uncertainty: Conclusions can change when new data arrives; that is how science works.

cards.body: Every instrument has limits. Scientists report how accurate a measurement is and how much it can vary.
cards.example: A sensor reading can be 'good' or 'fair' quality.
cards.title: Uncertainty and quality
cards.uncertainty: Uncertainty is normal and expected, not a mistake.

cards.body: Good science says what the evidence supports and what cannot yet be concluded. Every answer leads to a new question.
cards.example: A mission finding often suggests the next mission's objective.
cards.title: Evidence and open questions
cards.uncertainty: A finding is only as strong as the data behind it.

meta.note: Bundled offline educational content for Moon Run. No internet connection is required. Measurement values are labelled real / simplified / fictional. Simplified means rounded, representative, or scaled for gameplay.

earth_mars.finding: Away from Earth's protection, radiation levels are higher and there is no magnetic field to deflect solar particles.
earth_mars.limitations: A single journey samples only part of the path; solar activity also changes over time.
earth_mars.next_question: How does radiation along the route change with the Sun's activity cycle?
earth_mars.objective: Fly the direct route to Mars and survey the environment along the way.
earth_mars.question: What conditions does a spacecraft face on a long interplanetary journey?

earth_moon.finding: The Moon has no atmosphere and no global magnetic field, so its surface swings from very hot days to very cold nights.
earth_moon.limitations: A few measurements cannot map the whole surface or show how conditions change with the seasons.
earth_moon.next_question: How do temperatures change near the lunar poles, where the Sun barely rises?
earth_moon.objective: Deliver the first cargo to the lunar outpost and study the Moon's surface environment.
earth_moon.question: How does the Moon's lack of atmosphere affect its surface temperature?

moon_mars.finding: Mars has a very thin carbon-dioxide atmosphere and is very cold, yet it can still raise planet-wide dust storms.
moon_mars.limitations: Surface measurements from one place cannot describe the whole planet or its weather over a year.
moon_mars.next_question: How do atmospheric pressure and temperature change over a full Martian year?
moon_mars.objective: Refuel at the outpost and push on to Mars to compare a thin atmosphere with the airless Moon.
moon_mars.question: How thin is the Martian atmosphere, and why can dust storms still form?

moon_round.finding: Samples and measurements can be collected and returned, but a two-way trip costs far more fuel and supplies.
moon_round.limitations: Returned samples are powerful, but they are few compared with what a survey mission can gather.
moon_round.next_question: Which sites should a return mission sample to answer the biggest questions?
moon_round.objective: Touch down, collect samples, then bring the crew and data safely home.
moon_round.question: Can a two-way mission collect useful science without running out of resources?

bio.fact: Living organisms are studied in orbit to learn how biology behaves in space.
bio.failure: Food runs short and the crew loses a way to produce fresh nutrients during the mission.
bio.real: NASA's BioNutrients project grows nutrient-producing yeast on demand in space.
bio.reflection: Which food would be hardest to grow in space, and why?
bio.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
bio.subject: Biological research
bio.title: BioNutrients Bay
bio.what: Grows yeast and other organisms to produce nutrients for the crew.
bio.why: Long missions cannot carry all their food, so being able to grow nutrients on board matters.

comms.fact: Radio signals travel at the speed of light, so talking to a distant spacecraft is never instant.
comms.failure: Data cannot be transmitted home, and the spacecraft must operate autonomously.
comms.real: NASA's Deep Space Network uses large dish antennas around the world to talk to distant spacecraft.
comms.reflection: What should a spacecraft do if it cannot reach Earth for an hour?
comms.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
comms.subject: Ground stations and radio communication
comms.title: Communications Room
comms.what: Sends science data and telemetry to Earth and receives commands from mission control.
comms.why: Without a radio link, mission control cannot track the spacecraft and scientists never receive the data.

engines.fact: Rockets work best in space because there is no air drag to slow them down.
engines.failure: The spacecraft cannot change course or reach its target; it drifts along its current path.
engines.real: The Space Shuttle Main Engine and the Saturn V F-1 engines are examples of real rocket propulsion.
engines.reflection: If a spacecraft has no fuel left, can it still change direction? Why not?
engines.subject: Propulsion and thrust
engines.title: Engine Room
engines.what: Turns propellant into thrust to change the spacecraft's velocity and direction.
engines.why: In space there is no road to push against, so a spacecraft must carry its own propellant to change speed.

medbay.fact: Spaceflight health is measured, recorded and studied, just like any other science data.
medbay.failure: Crew health and morale drop, reducing what the crew can do on board.
medbay.real: ISS crews exercise about two hours a day and follow a strict medical monitoring plan.
medbay.reflection: Why do astronauts exercise every day in space?
medbay.source: Canadian Space Agency - Digital Games and Activities
medbay.subject: Human spaceflight
medbay.title: Medical Bay
medbay.what: Keeps the crew healthy and treats injuries and illness during the mission.
medbay.why: Weightlessness weakens bones and muscles, and a sick or injured crew member can endanger the mission.

oxygen.fact: An astronaut uses roughly 0.8 kg of oxygen per day, so life support has very little slack.
oxygen.failure: Oxygen falls and gas levels become dangerous. Humans cannot survive an unbreathable cabin.
oxygen.real: The ISS Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) recycles air and water for the crew.
oxygen.reflection: Why do you think recycling air matters more on a long mission than on a short one?
oxygen.subject: Life-support systems
oxygen.title: Oxygen Control
oxygen.what: Scrubs carbon dioxide out of the air and keeps a breathable oxygen level for the crew.
oxygen.why: Humans need a steady supply of oxygen and must remove the carbon dioxide they exhale, every minute of every day.

piloting.fact: Getting to another planet is about timing and speed, not driving in a straight line.
piloting.failure: Navigation errors waste fuel and can send the spacecraft to the wrong place.
piloting.real: NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) is used to design and plan real spacecraft trajectories.
piloting.reflection: Why is reaching a planet about timing and speed rather than steering like a car?
piloting.subject: Orbital mechanics
piloting.title: Cockpit / Navigation
piloting.what: Steers the spacecraft and computes its trajectory: where it is, how fast it goes and where it will be next.
piloting.why: Spacecraft travel along curved trajectories, so small changes in speed and direction matter a great deal.

repair.fact: Reliability engineers plan for failures before launch, so one fault does not end the mission.
repair.failure: Broken systems stay broken, and small faults can grow into big problems.
repair.real: The ISS carries spare orbital replacement units that astronauts can swap out during spacewalks.
repair.reflection: What would you pack as a spare part if you could only choose one?
repair.subject: Reliability engineering
repair.title: Repair Bay
repair.what: Uses spare parts and crew time to fix damaged systems.
repair.why: A single failed part can endanger a mission, so spacecraft carry spare parts and redundancy.

sensors.fact: A spectrometer splits light into colours to identify what a material is made of.
sensors.failure: The mission collects little or no scientific data, so there is nothing for scientists to analyse.
sensors.real: Mars orbiters and rovers carry instrument suites to measure atmospheres, surfaces and radiation.
sensors.reflection: If you could carry only two instruments to Mars, which would you pick and what would you learn?
sensors.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
sensors.subject: Scientific instruments
sensors.title: Science Laboratory
sensors.what: Runs the ship's instruments: cameras, thermal sensors, spectrometers, pressure sensors and magnetometers.
sensors.why: Instruments let scientists study a distant world's temperature, atmosphere, surface and magnetic field without going there.

shields.fact: Engineers aim to reduce crew radiation exposure over a whole mission, not to block every particle.
shields.failure: Instruments and electronics can be damaged by radiation and the crew can be exposed to harmful doses.
shields.real: Current spacecraft cannot use energy deflector shields; they use materials, sheltered zones and careful mission planning instead.
shields.reflection: Which would you protect first: the crew, the instruments, or the engines? Why?
shields.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
shields.subject: Radiation and spacecraft protection
shields.title: Shield Generator
shields.what: Represents the spacecraft's protective shell and radiation shielding that keep equipment and crew safe.
shields.why: Outside Earth's atmosphere, spacecraft face solar radiation, cosmic rays, extreme temperatures and micrometeoroids.

weapons.fact: The space station's robotic arm Canadarm2 has caught visiting cargo spacecraft that were flying at thousands of kilometers an hour.
weapons.failure: Without a working arm or beam, a crew has to find another way to move and catch cargo.
weapons.real: Real missions use robotic arms such as Canadarm2 and the Mars rover arms to grab, scoop and move things.
weapons.reflection: What tool would you build to pick up a floating toolbox in space?
weapons.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
weapons.subject: Reaching and grabbing things in space
weapons.title: Tractor Beam
weapons.what: In this game, the Tractor Beam grabs floating cargo and gives you a hint at Puzzle Gates. Real spacecraft use robot arms and magnets, like the Canadarm2 on the space station.
weapons.why: Spacecraft often need to grab, move or hold things safely. Robot arms and beams do the heavy lifting so astronauts do not have to.

facts: Outside a magnetic field, charged particles from the Sun arrive far more easily.
Micrometeoroids can hit a spacecraft at several kilometres per second.
anomaly.interpretation: Away from planetary protection the environment is harsher: more radiation and dust, and no magnetic field to deflect particles.
anomaly.limits: This scenario is fictional gameplay; the concepts are real.

observations.note: Game value for a solar particle event near the ship.
Game value for the local field far from any planet.
Solar wind is mostly hydrogen and helium.

anomaly.question: Why would a mission designer plan extra shielding for a long trip through deep space?
anomaly.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
anomaly.title: DEEP SPACE - ENVIRONMENTAL SURVEY

facts: Earth's magnetic field deflects many charged particles from the Sun.
A pressure of 101325 Pa is one standard atmosphere.
planet_earth.interpretation: Earth's thick atmosphere and strong magnetic field shield the surface. Comparing other worlds to Earth helps scientists understand them.

observations.note: Earth's magnetic field ranges roughly 25-65 uT.

planet_earth.question: Why does a thick atmosphere and a magnetic field make a planet more friendly to life?
planet_earth.title: EARTH - REFERENCE MEASUREMENT

facts: Mars is red because its soil contains iron oxide (rust).
Its atmosphere is roughly 95% carbon dioxide.
planet_mars.interpretation: Mars has a very thin atmosphere and its surface is extremely cold, so any spacecraft working there needs strong thermal protection.
planet_mars.limits: Simplified rounded averages; real values change with location and season.

observations.note: No strong global magnetic field; only weak crustal pockets.
Measured by the Curiosity rover's radiation detector.

planet_mars.question: Why might a spacecraft need special thermal protection when operating on Mars?
planet_mars.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
planet_mars.title: MARS - SURFACE OBSERVATION

facts: Sunlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon.
Apollo samples showed the Moon is made of rock similar to Earth's.
planet_moon.interpretation: Without an atmosphere to trap heat, the Moon swings from very hot days to very cold nights. There is no air to breathe.
planet_moon.limits: Simplified extremes; real surface temperatures vary with latitude.

observations.note: The Moon has essentially no atmosphere.

planet_moon.question: Why is the temperature difference between lunar day and night so extreme?
planet_moon.source: NASA - Design and Develop Science Missions
planet_moon.title: MOON - SURFACE OBSERVATION

combat_safety.text: Real space missions stay safe by planning ahead, not by fighting. Engineers protect spacecraft from dust, heat and radiation so the science can go on.

communications.text: Ground stations receive information from spacecraft and send commands.

data.text: Data is not the same as knowledge. Scientists analyse measurements to understand what they mean.

engineering.text: Adding equipment can improve a mission, but it can also increase mass and power requirements.

exploration.text: Instruments let scientists investigate distant environments without needing to visit them in person.

failure.text: An unexpected result can still teach scientists something if the data is carefully examined.

launch.text: A successful launch places a spacecraft on its way. The spacecraft must still complete its mission objectives.

life_support.text: Human spacecraft must maintain a safe environment for their crew.

mission_planning.text: Every mission starts with a question. Scientists define what they want to discover before choosing the spacecraft and instruments.

mission_safety.text: Radiation, extreme temperatures and micrometeoroids can affect spacecraft.

navigation.text: Spacecraft travel along trajectories. Position, velocity and direction all matter.

power.text: Scientific instruments, computers, communications and other spacecraft systems need electrical power.

reliability.text: Backup systems can help a spacecraft keep operating if one component fails.

signal_delay.text: Radio signals travel at the speed of light. Communication with distant spacecraft is not instantaneous.

uncertainty.text: Measurements have limits. Scientists consider accuracy, uncertainty and instrument capability.
